intro: This guide takes your group through “Samuel Ajayi Crowther (For Teens)” in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the true story of a Yoruba boy captured in a slave raid at about thirteen, freed from a slave ship by the Royal Navy, who grew up to help give his people the Bible in their own language and became the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. It is written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group.

Each session runs about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand if your group prefers. Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you. Do the activity, which takes about ten minutes. Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens, or nothing at all. The book does not soften hard things: the violence of a slave raid, families torn apart, a boy’s attempts to end his own life, kidnapping, a death in an escape, and racism inside the church. Read those parts steadily, point out the help the chapters themselves urge anyone struggling to seek, and never press anyone to share their own hurts aloud; personal reflection stays private. If a teen seems affected, check in quietly afterwards. Some in your group may have family histories touched by slavery, migration or racism, so speak with care, and keep returning to the book’s honest pattern: what was evil is called evil, and God is still at work.

weeks.summary: In 1821 raiders surrounded the Yoruba town of Osogun, and Ajayi, about thirteen, was led away with a rope around his neck along with his mother, sisters and a cousin; he never saw his father again. Sixteen years later, as a Christian, he called it an “unhappy” day because of all he lost, and a “blessed” one because it began the journey that brought him to Christ. Like Joseph, he held both halves together: what others meant for evil, God meant for good. The big idea: you can call something truly wrong and still hope that God is not finished with it.

memory_verse.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today.

activity.title: Both Halves of the Sentence
steps: Read Crowther’s phrase “the unhappy, but … blessed day” and Joseph’s words in Genesis 50:20.
As a group, talk about why “everything happens for a reason” can sound hurtful when someone is suffering.
Compare it with how Joseph and Crowther spoke: what do they admit, and what do they hope?
Each person writes privately two sentences about a hard thing, beginning “It was unhappy because …” and “God could still …”, leaving the second blank if it isn’t ready yet.
Keep the papers to look at again when the book is finished.

weeks.summary: Traded again and again, Ajayi was chained for market and sold to a woman taking him toward the Popo country, where slaves were sold to the Portuguese. In despair he tried several times to strangle himself but could not, and he was sold on until he reached the slave port of Lagos. Years later he wrote that the Lord, “while I knew Him not,” had delivered him from evil, and he asked forgiveness rather than hiding what he had done. The big idea: despair is real, but it is not the end of the story, and darkness brought into the light loses some of its power.

memory_verse.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

activity.title: Deliver Us from Evil
steps: Begin by saying plainly that this chapter is about a boy who wanted to end his life, and that anyone carrying thoughts like that should tell a safe person this week: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor or a crisis line.
As a group, list the safe people and places in your community someone could turn to, and write them where everyone can see.
Read Crowther’s sentence about being delivered from evil while he did not yet know God.
Pray the line “deliver us from evil” slowly together, leaving a moment of silence for each person to bring someone to mind.
Make sure everyone leaves knowing they can talk to you privately.

weeks.summary: In Lagos, Ajayi was bought by Portuguese traders and kept chained by the neck for nearly four months before being put on a slave ship with 186 others. That same evening, 7 April 1822, two Royal Navy warships captured the ship; the boys first thought the sailors were cannibals, until they found the “heads” were cannonballs and the meat was pork. Ajayi struck the captured Portuguese owner, and later, as a Christian, called it wicked rather than justice; he was landed free in Sierra Leone. The big idea: Christ came to set captives free, and real freedom is something other than revenge.

memory_verse.text: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound.

activity.title: Justice or Payback?
steps: Read the moment where Ajayi hits the Portuguese owner and how he later judged it.
In small groups, write four short everyday scenarios where someone wants to get even: a comeback, a cold shoulder, a screenshot, a rumour.
Sort each scenario into “this is justice,” “this is payback” or “hard to tell,” and say why.
Discuss: what would a better response look like in each case?
Ask everyone to notice privately one moment this week when they want payback, and to ask Crowther’s question before acting.

weeks.summary: Living with a missionary family at Bathurst, Ajayi learned so fast that within six months he read the New Testament and taught younger pupils; he was baptised in December 1825, describing his conversion simply as God opening his heart. He took the name Samuel Crowther but never stopped being Ajayi, signing himself Samuel Ajayi Crowther and spending his life on the Yoruba language. He learned to wear boots by walking round a room, became the first student at Fourah Bay, and in 1829 married Asano, also freed from a slave ship. The big idea: in Christ you become a new creation, not a different person; God frees who he made rather than erasing them.

memory_verse.text: Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.

activity.title: Free It or Use It?
steps: Read how Crowther kept the name Ajayi all his life.
Each person writes three things that come from their family, culture or language: a phrase, a tradition, a skill.
Next to each, write whether it is something Jesus wants to free them from, or something he wants to make new and use.
Invite a few volunteers to share one thing they think God wants to use.
Talk about why some people think following Jesus means becoming someone else, and what this chapter says instead.

weeks.summary: In 1841 Crowther joined a British expedition up the Niger River, where he taught, prayed and met Yoruba people for the first time in twenty years. Fever killed 42 of about 150 Europeans and the expedition was called a failure, but most of the Africans stayed well. Crowther wrote carefully that Africa “can chiefly be benefitted by her own Children,” and within two years he was ordained, though he did not feel qualified. The big idea: witness starts at home, and you can reach “your own” people more naturally than anyone from outside.

memory_verse.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.

activity.title: My Jerusalem
steps: Draw four circles inside each other and label them Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth.
Explain how Acts 1:8 moves outward from home, and how Crowther saw Africans as best placed to reach Africa.
Each person writes in their inner circle the names of three people who are “their own”: same school, team, family or language.
Pick one name privately and commit to pray for that person every day this week.
Ask: why did Crowther go even though he said he wasn’t qualified?

weeks.summary: Ordained in London in 1843, Crowther preached in Freetown to a packed church, but the question “Who maketh thee to differ?” filled him with shame, since everything that set him apart had been given to him. He held what was probably the first church service in Yoruba. When a Shango drummer told him Freetown’s Christians were the worst adulterers in town, Crowther admitted the charge was “too true” and answered only with patience and an even temper. The big idea: everything we have is received, and when critics of Christians are right, the best answer is honesty and a changed life.

memory_verse.text: For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?

activity.title: Fair Criticism
steps: In small groups, list common criticisms people make of Christians today.
Sort them into “mostly unfair,” “partly true” and “too true.”
For one “too true” item, discuss how Crowther responded to the drummer: no spin, just honesty and patience.
Each person writes privately whether that criticism is true of them, and one concrete way to answer it with their life this week.
Close by reading 1 Corinthians 4:7 and naming things each of us has received rather than earned.

weeks.summary: In 1846 Crowther reached Abeokuta, and within weeks learned his mother was alive; they met after twenty-five years, trembling and silent with tears, on the day the Christian Almanac’s text read, “Thou art the Helper of the fatherless.” She had spent much of that time enslaved, came to trust Christ, and was baptised Hannah in 1848. She released him to his work, saying he was now God’s servant. The big idea: God sees the oppressed, and sometimes, without any plan of ours, he restores what we thought was lost.

memory_verse.text: But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless.

activity.title: Helper of the Fatherless
steps: Read Crowther’s journal entry about meeting his mother again.
Ask: why does it matter that Psalm 10 says God sees the violent and the oppressed?
As a group, think about who in a school or church might be “fatherless” in some sense: alone, grieving, new, cut off from family. Do not name anyone.
Brainstorm practical things a teen could do for someone like that: a message, an invitation, time, a seat at lunch.
Each person writes privately one thing they will do for someone this week.

weeks.summary: When Crowther was born, Yoruba had hardly been written; he collected words, published the first Yoruba vocabulary by a native speaker, and did the largest share of a team translation of the Bible completed in 1884. Translating the Bible declared the language worthy to carry God’s word, so no one had to become English to become a Christian. At Windsor in 1851 he prayed the Lord’s Prayer in Yoruba for Queen Victoria by candlelight, and the chapter also notes the British attack on Lagos that followed and what he could not foresee about colonial rule. The big idea: from Pentecost on, God has spoken to people in their own language.

memory_verse.text: And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?

activity.title: Heart Language
steps: Ask who in the group speaks or has family who speak another language, and invite them to say “Our Father” or a short blessing in it if they wish.
Talk about why Yoruba was hard to write down and why Crowther thought the effort was worth it.
Discuss Lamin Sanneh’s point: what does translating the Bible say about a language and its people?
Ask: what are the everyday words you actually think in, and do you pray in them or in “church language”?
End with a short time where each person prays silently in the words they really think in.

weeks.summary: Crowther’s 1854 voyage up the Niger and Benue lost no one, unlike 1841, and in 1857 he left African workers to plant a mission at Onitsha. Then the steamer Dayspring was wrecked near Jebba, and fifty people waited a year on the riverbank; Crowther led prayers, began writing the Nupe language, protected a robbed woman, and talked gently with Muslim neighbours, believing kindness, not abuse, would lead them to read the Bible. By the end there were new missions and the start of a Nupe grammar. The big idea: we may be pressed and perplexed, but not crushed, and a wrecked plan can still be a fruitful year.

memory_verse.text: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.

activity.title: What to Do with the Year
steps: Read the account of the Dayspring wreck and list together what Crowther did during the year of waiting.
Each person writes privately one plan of theirs that has stalled or fallen apart.
Under it, write three useful things they could do right where they are stuck: learn something, help someone, build a friendship.
Circle one to do this week.
Discuss Crowther’s approach to his Muslim neighbours: what does kindness make possible that arguing does not?

weeks.summary: Henry Venn believed the Niger should have an African bishop, and the obvious man was Crowther, who refused, saying, “I am not worthy,” until Venn pleaded with him and he accepted with Eli’s words. In 1864 he was consecrated in Canterbury Cathedral as the first African bishop of the Anglican Church, though only over lands beyond British territory. He asked not to be called “My Lord,” treated the role as a weight, and returned to a Niger where there was still everything to do. The big idea: God lifts up the lowly, and a position is a responsibility to serve, not a crown to grab.

memory_verse.text: He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor.

activity.title: Weight, Not Crown
steps: Read Crowther’s words that he was now “a kind of landmark,” and any false step would hurt all the native churches.
In small groups, list leadership roles teens hold: captain, prefect, worship team, older sibling, group-chat admin.
For each, write one way someone could treat it as a crown and one way they could treat it as a weight carried for others.
Ask: what limits were placed on Crowther as bishop, and what does that say about attitudes in 1864?
Each person chooses one way to serve someone “below” them this week.

weeks.summary: In 1867 Crowther, his son Dandeson and a bricklayer were seized by a chief named Abokko, who believed Crowther owned the trading posts and demanded a huge ransom. Abokko’s household slaves secretly shared their own food, and Crowther called them “our ravens”; without a Bible on Sunday, he and Dandeson recited Scripture from memory, and Dandeson refused to leave his father. In the escape the vice-consul Fell was killed by an arrow, and Crowther said he would rather have died in his place. The big idea: God often provides through the least powerful people, and Someone did die in our place.

memory_verse.text: But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.

activity.title: Spot the Ravens
steps: Read how the slave boys and women in Abokko’s house fed Crowther and Dandeson.
As a group, list the “ravens” in a typical week: people with little status who quietly help, such as cleaners, cafeteria staff, bus drivers or a younger sibling.
Each person writes a short thank-you note to one real “raven” in their life, to give this week.
Talk about Crowther’s response to Fell’s death and how it points to Christ dying in our place.
Ask: when have you been a raven for someone, or when could you be?

weeks.summary: By the late 1870s the Niger mission had real problems: distant stations, some unfaithful workers, and a girl who died from the cruelty of two mission employees, and Crowther was too lenient a disciplinarian, though he dismissed agents and offered to step aside. In 1890 a new group of young English missionaries suspended African clergy, including his son, in his presence; years later the society’s own historian admitted they were “too severe,” while still blaming “racial weaknesses.” Crowther stayed bishop, accepted decisions he disagreed with, and backed the Delta churches in supporting themselves. The big idea: when wounds come from your own side, you can call wrong wrong without becoming like those who did it.

memory_verse.text: For it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it; it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me— then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend.

activity.title: Fair to Everyone
steps: Point out that the chapter refuses to tell this story one-sidedly, and ask the group why that matters.
Make two columns: “What Crowther got wrong” and “What was done wrong to him,” and fill them in from the chapter.
Discuss how racism, even among kind people, shaped what happened in 1890.
Each person writes privately about a time a fellow Christian hurt them, and one way they are tempted to hit back that they choose not to act on.
Close by asking whether anyone needs to put right a time they were too severe with someone else.

weeks.summary: In 1891 Crowther had a stroke and recovered at his daughter Abigail’s home in Lagos, still working and blessing new schoolmasters. A last, unsent letter did not defend himself or accuse anyone, and on 31 December he said “Good night” to Abigail and died half an hour later. His work looked dead, but the Yoruba Bible, the beginnings of written Igbo and Nupe, and the self-supporting Delta churches remained, and in 2014 an Archbishop of Canterbury said he had been wronged. The big idea: like a grain of wheat, a faithful life may bear its harvest after we are gone.

memory_verse.text: In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.

activity.title: How I Want to Be Remembered
steps: Read Crowther’s last words to Abigail and the list of what survived him.
Each person writes one sentence about how they want to be remembered by the people closest to them.
Under it, write one small, faithful thing that fits that sentence and could be done every day this week.
Invite anyone who kept their sentences from the first week to look again privately at their “God could still …” line.
Close by naming one moment in Crowther’s story that the group will remember.
